title: The Last Wolf
premise: Hazel Dunmore, exiled to the valley of Vell where magic cannot follow, has spent ten years forgetting who she was — until prayers in her village begin being answered by old gods that should be dead. When a wounded stranger arrives carrying a map of a country erased from every record, Hazel learns the gods are returning because their last door is closing, and only someone born of storm can open it. Pursued by the Church of the Quiet and haunted by memories she paid dearly to lose, Hazel must choose between the found family she built in silence and the truth of what she did to earn her exile. In the end, she reopens the door not to escape but to give the dying gods a place in the world again, sacrificing her own magic — and staying in Vell, finally by choice rather than sentence.
about_author: Rosalind Reyes is the pen name of a former cartographer who spent years mapping places that no longer exist, an obsession that seeps into every page of her fiction. She writes from a farmhouse at the edge of a real valley, where she insists the weather listens when she reads aloud.

chapters.title: The Valley That Forgets
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Ten years after exile, Hazel tends goats in Vell, where magic dies at the border stones. A prayer she mutters over a sick lamb is answered — impossibly, with rain. The emotional beat is unease: the safe numbness of her life has cracked, and something on the other side noticed.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Border Stones
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A bleeding stranger named Corren collapses at the boundary, clutching a map drawn on wolf-hide showing roads through a country called Averlaine — which officially never existed. Hazel hides him from the village elders. The beat is reluctant compassion stirring against her instinct for isolation.

chapters.title: What the Elders Know
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Village matriarch Odell recognizes the map and warns Hazel that questions brought the last exile's death. Meanwhile, more answered prayers ripple through Vell: bread multiplying, dead wells refilling. The beat is dread — the valley's protective silence is failing, and Hazel is its fault line.

chapters.title: The Wolf on the Wolf-Hide
chapters.summary: Corren's POV. Delirious, Corren remembers fleeing the Church of the Quiet, which burns anyone who remembers Averlaine. He reveals the map was his sister's, and she didn't survive. The beat is grief entwining with purpose; he sees in Hazel the storm-born mark the map requires.

chapters.title: Rain Where Rain Shouldn't Fall
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A localized storm follows Hazel like a dog, answering her moods. Odell confronts her with proof Hazel once commanded weather — memory Hazel traded away for exile. The beat is vertigo: her identity is a locked room, and the key is turning itself.

chapters.title: The Church Arrives Quietly
chapters.summary: Corren's POV. Inquisitor Maren Sloe enters Vell wearing a pilgrim's humility, asking gentle questions about answered prayers. Corren recognizes her and begs Hazel to run. The beat is paranoia tightening into certainty: kindness, here, is a hunting technique.

chapters.title: Odell's Bargain
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Odell offers to smuggle them out if Hazel swears never to return — protecting the valley by amputating herself from it. Hazel refuses; Vell is the only family she has left. The beat is loyalty hardening into defiance against the woman who raised her.

chapters.title: Crossing the Stones
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Under cover of Maren's sermon, Hazel and Corren cross the border stones — and Hazel's suppressed magic detonates back into her like floodwater. Memories return in fragments: a burning tower, a voice calling her name. The beat is painful rebirth; power and trauma arrive together.

chapters.title: Roads That Aren't There
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Following the wolf-hide map, they walk terrain that reshapes itself — Averlaine exists only where it is remembered. They meet Tam, a feral child who lives inside the country's memory and calls Hazel 'the last wolf.' The beat is wonder shadowed by wrongness.

chapters.title: Tam's Country
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam shows them Averlaine as it was: markets, bells, a palace of glass. But each remembered building costs Tam a real memory of their own. The beat is tenderness curdling into horror — Hazel realizes the whole country is being kept alive by a child paying in themselves.

chapters.title: Maren's Mercy
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren catches up and, instead of arresting them, shares her own history: she was Averlaine-born, and the Church saved her from remembering. She offers Hazel erasure in exchange for surrendering Corren. The beat is seduction — the offer is genuinely tempting, and honestly meant.

chapters.title: The Tower in the Storm
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A returned memory leads Hazel to the ruined tower from her fragments: this is where she sealed the gods' door ten years ago, trading her memories as payment. She understands now that she wasn't exiled — she sentenced herself. The beat is devastating self-recognition.

chapters.title: What Hazel Did
chapters.summary: Corren's POV. Full flashback: young Hazel, grieving her slaughtered family, blamed the indifferent gods and slammed their door shut, dooming Averlaine to be forgotten. Corren's family were among those erased. He learns this and says nothing. The beat is betrayal swallowed whole, loyalty and truth at war.

chapters.title: The Silence Between Them
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel confesses everything before Corren can weaponize it, offering him her life. Instead he asks her to help him reopen the door — not for forgiveness, but because his sister prayed there once. The beat is grace: forgiveness neither earned nor granted, but chosen anyway.

chapters.title: Tam Runs Out of Memory
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam begins forgetting how to speak, then how to see, spending themselves to hold Averlaine stable long enough for the door. Hazel takes Tam's hand and promises to remember for both of them. The beat is found family crystallizing under pressure of imminent loss.

chapters.title: Maren's Choice
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Ordered to burn Vell as collateral, Maren turns her fire on her own Church instead, buying Hazel time at the cost of her rank and likely her life. The beat is redemption without absolution — Maren chooses truth over the institution that made forgetting bearable.

chapters.title: The Door in the Glass Palace
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. At Averlaine's remembered heart, the door stands thin as paper. Opening it requires a storm-caller's full strength — enough to kill. Behind it, the old gods wait, starving and diminished, including the one whose indifference broke Hazel. The beat is terrible approach toward sacrifice.

chapters.title: Prayers Answered
chapters.summary: Climax, Hazel's POV. As Maren holds the Church back and Tam fades, Hazel calls the storm of her life and tears the door open. Face to face with the god she hated, she does not strike him down — she gives the gods the one thing they lost: a people who remember them. The beat is fury transmuted into mercy.

chapters.title: The Price of the Storm
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The door holds; the gods pour through into a world learning to pray again. Hazel's magic gutters out, leaving her ordinary, mortal, emptied. Tam survives, small and new-made, held by Corren. The beat is hollow aftermath — victory that feels like amputation.

chapters.title: Homecoming Without Exile
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel returns to Vell expecting banishment; instead Odell meets her at the stones, and the valley — now touched by returning gods — accepts her freely. Corren stays to rebuild Averlaine with Tam. The beat is bittersweet parting: family doesn't require shared walls.

chapters.title: The Lamb and the Rain
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Seasons later, Hazel farms the same valley, magicless, content. A child pilgrim arrives asking about the last wolf, and Hazel tells the story true, including her own guilt. The beat is integration — memory kept, guilt carried, identity no longer a locked room.

chapters.title: Where the Door Stands Open
chapters.summary: Final chapter, rotating POVs. On midsummer night, the border stones hum, rain falls gently in Vell, and somewhere far off a bell rings in rebuilt Averlaine. Hazel stands at the threshold, welcome on either side. The beat is quiet resolution: the door stays open, and so does she.
